comments.text: That 192bit memory bus limits the RX 5600 XT to 3GB/6GB/12GB. The RX 5600 XT uses 6x1GB GDDR6 memory modules with 32bit connections for each module. The RX 5500 XT 4GB model uses 4x1GB modules and the 8GB model uses 4x2GB modules.
comments.author: @likeclockwork6473

comments.text: If the RX 5600 XT used 2GB GDDR6 memory modules it would be a 12GB model. Weird memory configs are possible but require unique coding. Unified designs are easier to port code to and from.

comments.text: @likeclockwork6473  thank you for explanation, that's the same reason why old 1060 used 3 or 6gb cause it used 192-bit bus. I always questioned that because 4gigs on 1060 would make more sense.

comments.text: @nechastivi3187  Yep its the same thing with the old GTX 580. That had a 384 bit bus. That's 12 memory modules. 128MB each on the 1.5GB version and 256MB each on the 3GB version. The HD7970 had the same memory config. The R9 285 had 8x256MB modules, 2GB total. The R9 380 had this same config and 4GB models with 512MB modules. The GTX 280 and R9 290X had crazy 16 memory module configs

All this crap people are talking about this card is actually pretty unfounded. The card proves it can deliver a stable gaming performance for regular people who can't spring for a $400+ card. $200 isn't that huge of a price when you remember that all the premium cards these days are sitting around $700+. Should all graphics cards be cheaper right now? Definitely! Are they? Nope! This card does fine in gaming for regular people still rocking a 60hz 1080p display, to call the card bad simply  because it's a couple frames slower then another low end graphics card is just asinine. Furthermore, the thing this card still has 8GB of DDR6 memory & Freesync technology. Freesync being the big hit here because Freesync monitors are cheaper and deliver a smoother picture then gsync ones, meaning thos extra couple of frames the nvidia alternative gets you means absolutely nothing if all you're seeing is a choppy mess to begin with. It does better then the GTX 1060 6GB (EVGA) that's currently in my computer. Another card that handles most games fairly well so long as you actually take the time to configure your graphic settings properly. For people getting into computers for the first time, know this, THERE IS NOTHING WRONG WITH THIS CARD.


 If you buy a decent x570 motherboard and combine it with either a Ryzen 7 2700x or Ryzen 5 3600x (If money is tight get a first gen Ryzen 5 1500x or better), some DDR4 3200 memory (I recommend an 8GB single stick or dual 4GB sticks if money is tight and double it later, of the same exact model, do not mix and match ram as it creates stability issues, 2400 speed memory is as low as you should go with DDR4 but I recommend going straight for 3200 as you can find 16GB of it for about $75 on newegg [RGB even]) and an m.2 NVME SSD (I recommend the 1TB Intel 660p as it has capacity and is only about $100, you can get 4TB 7200rpm [stay away from 5400rpm drives, they will take forever to transfer files and trying to run even the simplest of games off of one if you should need to will be a headache] HDD to go with it if you need extra storage space for around $90 each ) and for power I recommend not getting anything below a 600w 80+ Bronze power supply. This card will compliment the build nicely and please do not cheap out on your case, cheap cases can be dangerous for your hardware, I know that $25 case price is tempting but those cases are often not properly grounded and can kill your system. If you're really, really strapped for cash then cheap out on the CPU before anything else, they are the easiest and cheapest component to upgrade down the road. I hope my little guide is helpful to newcomers, I've been building are repairing computers for 16 years and have always focused on making the best systems possible without spending a ton of money. Many of these tech youtuber channels are run by people who have become spoiled by top tier parts and forget what it means to find the best bang for your buck.
